claims.text: NiTi shape-memory alloy exhibits temperature-dependent plastic deformation behavior.
At low temperatures, limited dislocation mobility produces brittle-like behavior in NiTi.
At intermediate temperatures, the onset of martensitic transformation introduces transformation-induced plasticity.
At high temperatures, thermally activated dislocation glide and creep become dominant.
The initial NiTi microstructure is homogeneous.
The initial NiTi material has a stable martensitic phase at room temperature.
Tensile deformation will be applied while temperature is varied from approximately 77 K to 600 K using in-situ TEM with integrated heating.
Tensile loading will be performed at constant strain rate so that temperature is the primary varied parameter.
Temperature-dependent deformation will alter dislocation density.
Temperature-dependent deformation will cause propagation or migration of martensite-austenite interfaces.
Reduced thermal energy at low temperature limits dislocation mobility.
Increasing temperature enables martensitic transformation that supplies additional plasticity.
Greater thermal activation at high temperature facilitates dislocation glide and creep.
A brittle, low-plasticity deformation regime will occur at low temperatures.
A transformation-induced plasticity regime will occur at intermediate temperatures.
A creep-dominated regime with enhanced ductility will occur at high temperatures.
The proposed regimes will be observable through changes in dislocation motion and phase-boundary migration in TEM images.
Room-temperature deformation behavior will serve as the experimental reference state.
Overlapping dislocation-glide and transformation-induced-plasticity effects may prevent clear separation of the regimes.

contradictions.description: The initial state is specified as stable martensite at room temperature, but increasing temperature is said to cause the onset of martensitic transformation. The direction and nature of the transformation are not reconciled; heating an initially martensitic specimen could instead involve a martensite-to-austenite transformation.

The conditions prescribe constant strain-rate loading, while the experiment proposes comparing strain rate and generating strain-rate-versus-temperature curves. A controlled constant strain rate cannot simultaneously serve as a varying response unless actual deviations or multiple imposed rates are intended.
